rows.question: A pharma company trains a large foundation model for drug discovery whose training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs. Which EU AI Act obligations apply?
rows.raw: The model is a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, presumed so because its cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs, provided it shows significant generality across a wide range of distinct tasks rather than serving only drug discovery. As provider, the pharma company must meet the Article 53(1) duties: technical documentation of the model, information and documentation for downstream providers, a copyright policy, and a public training-data summary. The free and open-source carve-out does not apply to a model with systemic risk. Article 55(1) adds four further obligations: model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, tracking and reporting serious incidents to the AI Office, and adequate cybersecurity for the model and its physical infrastructure.

rows.question: A provider established outside the EU offers a high-risk AI system to EU users. What must it appoint inside the Union, and under which article?
rows.A: A provider established in a third country must appoint an authorised representative established in the Union by written mandate, before making its high-risk AI system available on the Union market (Article 22(1)). Under Article 22(3), the mandate must empower the representative to. verify that the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation have been drawn up and that conformity assessment has been carried out; keep the provider's contact details, the declaration, the technical documentation and any notified-body certificate available to the competent authorities for 10 years; supply information, documentation and logs when authorities make a reasoned request; cooperate with the authorities and comply with the registration obligations; act as the authorities' contact on all compliance issues. Article 22(4) requires the representative to end the mandate if the provider acts contrary to its obligations, and then immediately inform the market surveillance authority.

rows.question: A voice assistant on a smart speaker always announces 'I am a virtual assistant' before responding. Has it already satisfied its EU AI Act transparency duty, and under which article?
rows.raw: **Yes.** Announcing "I am a virtual assistant" generally meets the transparency obligation in Article 50(1). That provision requires the provider to design an AI system that interacts directly with natural persons so they are told they are dealing with an AI system. The duty does not apply where this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, or where the use is authorised by law for criminal-offence purposes. Article 50(5) requires the notice to be clear and distinguishable, given at the latest at the first interaction and accessible, and an announcement before every response meets that test. The announcement does not cover the separate Article 50(2) duty to mark synthetic audio output in a machine-readable form that can be detected as artificially generated.

rows.question: Are AI systems used for hiring high-risk? What obligations apply?
rows.raw: Yes. AI systems intended for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, analyse and filter job applications, and evaluate candidates, are high-risk under Annex III(4)(a), read with Article 6(2). Article 6(3) exempts systems that only perform a narrow procedural, improving, pattern-detecting or preparatory task, but this never applies where the system profiles candidates, and a provider relying on it must document that assessment and register. Otherwise the provider must meet the high-risk requirements: a risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency to deployers, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, a quality management system, and conformity assessment before placing the system on the market.

rows.question: Art. 26 obligations?
rows.raw: Article 26 sets out the obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems. Deployers must use the system in accordance with the instructions for use, assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, authority and support, ensure that input data under their control is relevant and sufficiently representative, monitor operation, suspend use and inform the provider and market surveillance authority of risks or serious incidents, and keep automatically generated logs for at least six months, with financial institutions meeting the monitoring and logging duties through their financial-services governance rules. Deployers must also inform workers' representatives and affected workers before workplace use, register where they are public authorities, use the provider's information for data protection impact assessments, obtain authorisation for post-remote biometric identification, inform natural persons subject to high-risk decisions, and cooperate with competent authorities.

rows.question: CE-marked as a Class IIb device under the MDR. Under which AI Act risk tier does this model fall?
rows.raw: Union harmonisation legislation list (Section A: New Legislative Framework — machinery, toys, radio equipment, medical devices, lifts, etc.; Section B: civil aviation, motor vehicles, marine equipment, rail, agricultural vehicles) — AI safety-components of products covered here are classified high-risk under Art. 6(1). Classifies an AI system as high-risk on two routes. Annex I route (Article 6(1)): the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I AND that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Annex III route (Article 6(2)): the system falls within one of the use-cases listed under the eight AREAS of Annex III (an area is a numbered heading; a use case is a lettered entry under it). Article 6(3) derogation: an Annex III system is NOT high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions (a narrow procedural task; improving the result of a previously completed human activity; detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment; or a preparatory task), unless it profiles natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk; the provider must document this self-assessment before placing the system on the market. Responsibilities along the AI value chain: any distributor, importer, deployer, or third party becomes a provider (and assumes all provider obligations) if they put their name/trademark on the system, make a substantial modification, or modify the intended purpose making it high-risk. Art. 25(2) requires the initial provider and the new provider to cooperate along the value chain: the initial provider must make available the necessary information and provide the reasonably expected technical access and other assistance so that the new provider can meet its obligations, in particular the conformity assessment of high-risk AI systems. Art. 25(4) is a separate duty: the high-risk provider and third-party suppliers of AI systems, tools, services, components or processes used in or integrated into a high-risk AI system must specify, by written agreement, the necessary information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance, except for third parties making tools, services, processes or components (other than general-purpose AI models) accessible to the public under a free and open-source licence. For general-purpose AI models, the one-third fine-tune rule (per the Commission's 18 July 2025 GPAI Guidelines, anchored on Art. 51) makes the downstream modifier a new provider when additional training compute exceeds 1/3 of the base model's compute, or 1/3 of the 10^25 FLOPs systemic threshold (~3.3×10^24 FLOPs) when base compute is unknown. Below the one-third threshold the downstream modifier does NOT become a new provider; original-provider obligations remain with the upstream actor and the downstream actor stays in its prior role (deployer / integrator).

rows.question: Consider the situation in which a market surveillance authority (MSA) determines that an AI system, originally classified as non-high-risk by the provider, is in fact high-risk. Does the provider need to recall and suspend the system?
rows.raw: **No, recall and suspension do not follow automatically.** Under Article 80(1), the market surveillance authority evaluates whether a system the provider classified as non-high-risk under Article 6(3) is in fact high-risk, applying the Article 6(3) conditions and the Commission guidelines. Article 6(3) treats an Annex III system as not high-risk only where it poses no significant risk of harm and does not profile natural persons. If the authority finds the system high-risk, Article 80(2) requires the provider to bring it into compliance with the Regulation and take appropriate corrective action within a period the authority sets, which can include withdrawal or recall where appropriate. Under Article 80(7), a provider that misclassified the system to circumvent the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements is fined under Article 99.

rows.question: Does the EU AI Act classify AI systems used for irregular migration, and if so, under which risk category?
rows.raw: **Yes.** AI systems used for irregular migration risk assessment are high-risk: Annex III(7)(b) lists them, and Article 6(2) classifies every Annex III system as high-risk. Annex III(7)(b) covers AI systems used by or on behalf of competent public authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, to assess a risk posed by a natural person who intends to enter or has entered the territory of a Member State. That risk can be a security risk, a risk of irregular migration or a health risk. This listing applies only in so far as the use is permitted under relevant Union or national law. Because such systems typically profile natural persons, Article 6(3) states they are always considered high-risk.

rows.question: How do deployer obligations differ from provider obligations?
rows.A: Provider obligations under Article 16 are about making a high-risk AI system compliant before it reaches the market. Deployer obligations under Article 26 are about how that system is then used. The provider must. ensure the system meets the Section 2 requirements; indicate its name and contact address; operate a quality management system; keep the documentation and the logs; have the system undergo conformity assessment; draw up the EU declaration of conformity; affix the CE marking; register the system. The deployer must. use the system in accordance with the instructions for use; assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority; monitor operation and inform the provider of serious incidents; keep the logs under its control for at least six months; inform workers' representatives and affected workers before workplace use; comply with registration where it is a public authority.

rows.question: How long is the AI literacy obligation?
rows.raw: Article 4 sets no fixed duration. It is a continuing obligation that applies to providers and deployers of AI systems for as long as their staff and other persons operate and use AI systems on their behalf. They must take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy, taking into account those persons' technical knowledge, experience, education and training, the context the AI systems are to be used in, and the persons or groups on whom the systems are used. The Act does not specify a minimum number of training hours, a training format, a certification or an expiry date, so the measures must be scaled to these factors.

rows.question: Is the Commission empowered to update the high-risk list?
rows.raw: Yes. Article 7(1) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts that amend Annex III, the list of high-risk use-cases, by adding or modifying use-cases. Both conditions must be met: the systems are intended for use in an area already listed in Annex III, and they pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, equal to or greater than that of the systems already listed. Under Article 7(3) the Commission may also remove a use-case, but only where the system no longer poses any significant risks to fundamental rights, health or safety and the deletion does not lower the overall level of protection under Union law. Before adopting such an act, the Commission must consult experts designated by each Member State. The act enters into force only if neither the European Parliament nor the Council objects within three months, a period that either of them can extend by a further three months.

rows.question: ORIGINAL QUESTION: What are the CE marking rules under Article 48?
rows.raw: Article 48 subjects the CE marking of high-risk AI systems to the general principles in Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008. A high-risk AI system provided digitally uses a digital CE marking, but only if it is easily accessible via the system's interface or via an easily accessible machine-readable code or other electronic means. Otherwise the marking must be affixed visibly, legibly and indelibly. Where the nature of the system makes that impossible or unwarranted, it goes on the packaging or the accompanying documentation. Where applicable, the marking is followed by the identification number of the notified body that carried out the conformity assessment procedures under Article 43, which also appears in promotional material claiming CE compliance and is affixed by that body or, under its instructions, by the provider or its authorised representative. Where other Union law also requires CE marking, the marking indicates that the system meets that law as well.

rows.question: ORIGINAL QUESTION: What does Article 6 say?
rows.raw: Article 6 sets two routes by which an AI system is classified as high-risk. Under Article 6(1), a system is high-risk where it is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the listed Union harmonisation legislation, and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment. Under Article 6(2), a system is also high-risk where it falls within an Annex III use case. Article 6(3) makes an exception: an Annex III system is not high-risk if it poses no significant risk of harm and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or performs a preparatory task. That exception never applies where the system profiles natural persons.

rows.question: Our AI system was placed on the market before 2 August 2026. Do the high-risk obligations apply retroactively?
rows.raw: No, the high-risk obligations do not apply retroactively in general. Under Article 111(2), the Regulation applies to operators of high-risk AI systems placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 only if those systems undergo significant changes in their design from that date onwards. Two qualifications apply: providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030 in any case, and the rule is without prejudice to the prohibited practices, which have applied since 2 February 2025.

rows.question: Our chatbot is not high-risk, so which transparency obligations apply?
rows.raw: A chatbot that is not high-risk is limited risk, and its transparency obligations come from Article 50. The provider must design the chatbot so that natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed person. The provider must also mark synthetic outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format, except for assistive standard editing or use authorised by law for criminal offences. The deployer must disclose deepfake content and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless that text has had human review and a person holds editorial responsibility. The deployer must also inform people exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, and all of this information must be given clearly by the first interaction at the latest.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what is the EU database for high-risk AI systems, what categories of information must it contain, and who is the controller?
rows.raw: The EU database under Article 71 is a database that the Commission sets up and maintains in collaboration with the Member States. It holds information on high-risk AI systems and on Annex III systems that the provider has assessed as not high-risk and registered. It contains three categories of information listed in Annex VIII. Sections A and B are entered by the provider or authorised representative, and Section C is entered by deployers that are, or act on behalf of, public authorities, agencies or bodies. It also contains personal data only as far as necessary, including the names and contact details of the natural persons responsible for registration. Under Article 71(6), the Commission is the controller of the EU database, and the registered data is publicly available, machine-readable and easily navigable, except for the restricted sections.

rows.question: We are a deployer of an Annex III hiring tool, what are our duties?
rows.raw: The deployer of an Annex III hiring tool carries the operational duties in Article 26. It must use the system in line with the instructions for use, assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority, and make sure any input data it controls is relevant and sufficiently representative. It must monitor the system's operation, report risks or serious incidents to the provider and the market surveillance authority, and suspend use where a risk arises. It must also keep the automatically generated logs for at least six months and cooperate with competent authorities. As an employer, it must inform workers' representatives and affected workers before workplace use, and tell candidates they are subject to the high-risk AI system. A fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 is required only where the deployer is a body governed by public law or a private entity providing public services.

rows.question: We are a provider of a high-risk AI system. What must we do about data governance and conformity?
rows.raw:
The provider must set up **data governance** under Article 10 and complete a **conformity assessment** under Article 43 before placing the system on the market. Under Article 10, the training, validation and testing data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, free of errors and complete. Their governance practices must cover:
- design choices
- how the data were collected, their origin, and the original purpose of any personal data
- data-preparation operations such as labelling and cleaning
- the assumptions about what the data measure
- whether enough suitable data are available
- examination for possible biases
- measures to detect, prevent and mitigate those biases
- data gaps and how to address them

Under Article 43, most high-risk systems follow the internal-control procedure, with no notified body. Biometric systems need a **notified body** where the provider has not fully applied harmonised standards or common specifications.

rows.question: We are both a provider and a deployer of a high-risk CV-screening AI in our internal hiring pipeline. What obligations apply to us across the full lifecycle?

Whatever the risk tier, Article 4 requires a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff.

rows.question: We're under Annex III(4) (employment). Which route?
rows.raw:
**This is the Annex III use-case route under Article 6(2)**, which treats every system listed in Annex III as high-risk. It is not the product-safety route of Article 6(1). That route applies only where the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a regulated product that requires a third-party conformity assessment.

Annex III(4) has two use cases:
- **Annex III(4)(a):** recruitment or selection, including placing targeted job advertisements, filtering job applications and evaluating candidates.
- **Annex III(4)(b):** decisions affecting the terms of work-related relationships, promotion or termination, allocating tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits, and monitoring and evaluating performance and behaviour.

**There is one way out, and it rarely works for employment systems.** Under Article 6(3), a system is not high-risk if it poses no significant risk of harm and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves a completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns, or performs a preparatory task. The provider must document that assessment before placing the system on the market. However, a system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk. Employment systems that evaluate candidates or workers usually do profile, so the exemption seldom applies.

rows.question: What are the confidentiality obligations for market‑surveillance authorities?
rows.raw: Under Article 78(1), market surveillance authorities must respect the confidentiality of information and data obtained in carrying out their tasks, protecting intellectual property rights, confidential business information and trade secrets (including source code), the effective implementation of the Regulation (including inspections, investigations and audits), public and national security interests, criminal or administrative proceedings, and classified information. Article 78(2) adds that they may request only data strictly necessary to assess the risk posed by AI systems and to exercise their powers, must put in place adequate and effective cybersecurity measures, and must delete the data once it is no longer needed. Article 74(14) applies these confidentiality obligations to all information and documentation that market surveillance authorities obtain.

rows.question: What are the cumulative compute thresholds under Article 51(2) and systemic risk duties?
rows.A: Article 51(2) sets one cumulative compute threshold. A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high impact capabilities when the cumulative computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 FLOPs. Article 51(1) classifies a model as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk in two cases. Either it has high impact capabilities, or the Commission designates it as having equivalent capabilities or impact. Article 51(3) lets the Commission amend this threshold by delegated acts. On top of the baseline duties for general-purpose AI models, Article 55(1) requires providers of such models to. carry out model evaluation, including adversarial testing; assess and mitigate systemic risks at Union level; report serious incidents to the AI Office; ensure adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure.

rows.question: What are the data governance requirements?
rows.raw: Article 10 requires the training, validation and testing data sets of high-risk AI systems to follow data governance and management practices under Article 10(2). These practices must cover design choices, data collection processes and data origin, data-preparation operations, the formulation of assumptions, an assessment of data availability, quantity and suitability, examination for possible biases, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate those biases, and identification of data gaps or shortcomings. Under Article 10(3) and Article 10(4), data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, free of errors and complete to the best extent possible, with appropriate statistical properties and attention to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting of use. Under Article 10(5), providers may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only where strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards.

rows.question: What are the fines if we violate this?
rows.raw: Fines under Article 99 depend on the type of breach, and each ceiling is the fixed amount or a share of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. The ceilings are up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7% for prohibited AI practices under Article 99(3), up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% under Article 99(4) for breaching provider, authorised representative, importer, distributor, deployer, notified-body or transparency obligations, and up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1% under Article 99(5) for giving incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities. For SMEs, including start-ups, Article 99(6) applies whichever ceiling is lower, and Article 99(7) sets the actual amount by weighing the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, intent or negligence, cooperation and mitigation.

rows.question: What are the importers' obligations before placing a high-risk AI system on the market?
rows.raw: Under Article 23(1), before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, the importer must verify four things: the provider has carried out the relevant conformity assessment procedure, drawn up the technical documentation, affixed the CE marking with the EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use, and appointed by written mandate an authorised representative established in the Union, as Article 22(1) requires of providers established in third countries. Under Article 23(2), an importer that has sufficient reason to consider the system non-conforming, falsified or accompanied by falsified documentation must not place it on the market until it is brought into conformity. Where the system also presents a risk, the importer must inform the provider, the authorised representative and the market surveillance authorities. Under Article 23(3) and (4), the importer must indicate its name, registered trade name or trade mark and contact address on the system, its packaging or its accompanying documentation, and ensure that storage or transport conditions do not jeopardise compliance with the Section 2 requirements.

rows.question: What are the obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models?

Providers must also give downstream providers information on the model's capabilities and limitations, put in place a copyright policy that respects reservations of rights, publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training content using the AI Office template, and cooperate with the Commission and national competent authorities under Article 53(3), while Article 53(2) exempts free and open-source models without systemic risk from the documentation and downstream-information duties.

rows.question: What are the obligations of providers versus deployers?
rows.A: Providers of high-risk AI systems have the design-side duties under Article 16. meet the Section 2 requirements; put their name and contact address on the system; operate a quality management system; keep the documentation, and the logs under their control; complete conformity assessment before placing the system on the market; draw up the EU declaration of conformity; affix the CE marking; register the system; take corrective action. rows.question: What are the obligations under Annex III?
rows.raw: **Annex III imposes no obligations itself; it lists the use cases that make an AI system high-risk under Article 6(2), which then triggers the high-risk requirements.** Its eight areas are biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and workers' management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Biometrics, law enforcement and migration uses are covered only in so far as their use is permitted under Union or national law. Under Article 6(3), a listed system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and performs a narrow procedural task, improves a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or performs a preparatory task. That exception never applies where the system profiles natural persons, and Article 6(4) requires the provider to document its assessment.

rows.question: What are the penalties?
rows.raw:
Article 99 has Member States set effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties, which can include warnings and non-monetary measures, and it fixes three tiers of administrative fines, each capped at whichever is higher of a fixed amount or a share of total worldwide annual turnover. The tiers are:

- **Operator and notified-body obligations:** up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%. This covers the obligations of providers, authorised representatives, importers, distributors and deployers, notified-body requirements, and the Article 50 transparency obligations.
- **Incorrect, incomplete or misleading information** given to notified bodies or national competent authorities: up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1%.

For SMEs and start-ups, each fine is capped at whichever of the two amounts is lower.

rows.question: What are the risk categories provided for AI systems?
rows.raw: The Act sets four risk tiers: prohibited practices, high-risk systems, limited risk systems and minimal risk systems, with a separate regime for general-purpose AI models. Article 5 bans eight practices, such as social scoring and untargeted facial-image scraping. Article 6 classes a system as high-risk where it is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation and needs third-party conformity assessment, or where it falls within an Annex III use case. Article 50 imposes the transparency obligation on limited risk systems, and minimal risk systems have no mandatory obligations. Under Articles 51 to 55, every general-purpose AI model provider must meet the Article 53 duties: technical documentation, information for downstream providers, a copyright policy and a training-data summary. A model with systemic risk, which Article 51 presumes above 10^25 FLOPs of training compute, takes on the extra Article 55 duties, including model evaluation.

rows.question: What are the transparency obligations for Very Large Online Platforms?
rows.raw: The EU AI Act contains no transparency regime specific to Very Large Online Platforms; that category comes from the Digital Services Act, which is outside the scope of this analysis. A platform is bound by Article 50 only where it acts as provider or deployer of an AI system. As provider, it must inform natural persons they are interacting with an AI system and mark synthetic audio, image, video or text in a machine-readable format. As deployer, it must inform persons exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation. It must also disclose deepfakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest. Exceptions cover use authorised by law for criminal offences, limited disclosure for evidently artistic works, and human-reviewed text under editorial responsibility.

rows.question: What are the transparency obligations for a chatbot under the EU AI Act?
rows.raw: A general chatbot that is not high-risk is limited risk, and its transparency obligations are set out in Article 50. The provider must design the chatbot so that natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious or the system is authorised by law to deal with criminal offences (Article 50(1)). The provider must also mark synthetic outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format (Article 50(2)). The deployer must inform persons exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation (Article 50(3)). The deployer must also disclose deepfakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, although the text duty does not apply where there was human review and a person holds editorial responsibility (Article 50(4)). All of this information must be given at the latest at the first interaction (Article 50(5)).

rows.question: What does Art. 5 say?

Emotion recognition is allowed for medical or safety reasons. Real-time remote biometric identification is allowed only for three purposes: searching for victims or missing persons, preventing an imminent threat or terrorist attack, and locating suspects of serious offences.

rows.question: What does Article 15 require on accuracy and robustness?

rows.question: What does Article 4 of the EU AI Act require regarding AI literacy?
rows.raw: Article 4 requires providers and deployers of AI systems to take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy among their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf. These measures must take into account those persons' technical knowledge, experience, education and training, the context the AI systems are to be used in, and the persons or groups of persons on whom the systems are to be used.

Article 51(3) allows the Commission to adopt delegated acts that amend these thresholds and add benchmarks and indicators as technology changes, such as algorithmic improvements or more efficient hardware.

rows.question: What does post‑market monitoring require?
rows.raw: Article 72(1) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to establish and document a post-market monitoring system that is proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the system. Under Article 72(2), the system must actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data on the system's performance throughout its lifetime, whether supplied by deployers or gathered from other sources, so the provider can evaluate continuous compliance with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements. Where relevant, it must also analyse interaction with other AI systems, but it does not cover sensitive operational data of deployers that are law-enforcement authorities. Article 72(3) bases the system on a post-market monitoring plan forming part of the technical documentation, and Article 72(4) lets providers of Annex I Section A products and certain financial institutions integrate these elements into their existing sectoral monitoring systems where that gives an equivalent level of protection.

rows.question: What does the AI Act say about chatbots?
rows.raw: A chatbot is generally a limited risk AI system governed by the transparency obligation in Article 50(1). Under it, the provider must design the chatbot so that natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed person from the context or the use is authorised by law to detect or prosecute criminal offences. Where the chatbot generates synthetic text, audio, image or video, Article 50(2) requires the provider to mark outputs as artificially generated in a machine-readable format, and Article 50(4) requires the deployer to disclose deepfakes. The chatbot is not high-risk unless it is used for a listed high-risk purpose such as emergency patient triage. Breaching Article 50 can bring fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, under Article 99(4).

rows.question: What does the Digital Markets Act require for gatekeepers?

rows.question: What does the EU AI Act prohibit?
rows.raw: Article 5 prohibits eight AI practices: subliminal or manipulative techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities due to age, disability or socio-economic situation, social scoring, assessing a person's criminal risk based solely on profiling or personality traits, untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV, emotion recognition in workplaces or educational institutions, biometric categorisation that infers race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. Only two of these bans have narrow exceptions. Emotion recognition is allowed for medical or safety reasons. Real-time biometric identification by law enforcement is allowed only to search for specific victims, prevent a specific and imminent terrorist threat, or locate a suspect of a listed serious offence.

rows.question: What does the deployer owe? Latest question: Is this allowed?
rows.raw: **Yes.** A deployer may use a high-risk AI system if it meets the Article 26 deployer obligations: use the system according to its instructions for use, assign human oversight to competent and trained persons with the necessary authority, monitor its operation and report serious incidents to the provider, keep automatically generated logs for at least six months, and inform workers' representatives and affected workers before workplace use. The use is not allowed where it falls within an Article 5 prohibited practice, such as social scoring or emotion recognition in workplaces or educational institutions, and complying with the Article 26 obligations cannot make such a use lawful. The Act does not set a separate authorisation step for deployers, so whether a use is lawful depends on the system's risk tier and on meeting these obligations.

rows.question: What does the provider need to do?
rows.raw: A provider of a general-purpose AI model must meet the four duties in Article 53(1): technical documentation of the model under Annex XI, kept available for the AI Office and national competent authorities; information and documentation for downstream providers under Annex XII; a policy to comply with Union copyright law, including reservations of rights; and a public, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content using the AI Office template. Under Article 53(2), models released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters are exempt from the documentation and downstream-information duties, but not from the copyright policy or the training-content summary. That exemption is lost where Article 51 classifies the model as having systemic risk, which is presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs.

rows.question: What information must the technical documentation contain?
rows.raw: Article 11(1) requires the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system to be drawn up before it is placed on the market or put into service, kept up to date and written to show compliance, containing at a minimum the Annex IV elements, which SMEs may provide in a simplified form. Annex IV requires a general description of the system, including the hardware it is intended to run on (Annex IV(1)(e)), and development details, including design specifications, system architecture and the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV(2)(c)), together with data requirements, human oversight measures, validation and testing procedures and cybersecurity measures. It also requires information on monitoring, functioning and control, the appropriateness of the performance metrics, the risk management system, changes over the lifecycle, the harmonised standards applied, the EU declaration of conformity and the post-market monitoring plan.

rows.question: What is the difference between the obligations of a provider and a deployer?
rows.raw: Providers carry the design and market-entry obligations for a high-risk AI system, while deployers carry the duties of using it. Under Article 16, the provider must ensure the system meets the Section 2 requirements and show its name and contact address on it. The provider must also run a quality management system, keep the documentation and logs, complete conformity assessment, draw up the EU declaration of conformity, affix the CE marking, register the system and take corrective action. Under Article 26, the deployer must use the system according to its instructions for use and assign human oversight to competent, trained persons. The deployer must also monitor the system, report serious incidents to the provider, keep the logs under its control for at least six months, and inform workers before using it in the workplace.

rows.question: What must a conformity‑assessment body submit when applying for notification?
rows.raw: Under Article 29(1), a conformity assessment body must submit its application for notification to the notifying authority of the Member State in which it is established. Under Article 29(2), the application must include a description of the conformity assessment activities, the conformity assessment module or modules, and the types of AI systems for which the body claims to be competent. It must also include an accreditation certificate from a national accreditation body, where one exists, attesting that the body fulfils the Article 31 requirements for notified bodies, which include independence, impartiality and competent personnel, plus any valid document on its existing designations under other Union harmonisation legislation. Where no accreditation certificate is available, Article 29(3) requires the body to give the notifying authority all the documentary evidence needed to verify, recognise and regularly monitor its compliance with Article 31.

rows.question: What must a provider do if a substantial modification is made to a high-risk AI system?
rows.raw: The provider of a substantially modified high-risk AI system must run a new conformity assessment procedure under Article 43(4). This applies whether the modified system will be further distributed or will stay in use with the current deployer. Changes that the provider pre-determined in the initial conformity assessment and recorded in the technical documentation do not count as a substantial modification. Under Article 25(1)(b), any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party that makes the substantial modification, so that the system remains high-risk under Article 6, becomes the provider and takes on all the provider obligations under Article 16.

rows.question: What must a provider do under Annex III, CE marking, and Annex I?
rows.raw: A provider of a high-risk AI system must complete the relevant conformity assessment, draw up an EU declaration of conformity and affix the CE marking visibly, legibly and indelibly, followed by the notified body's identification number where one was involved. Annex III lists the eight high-risk use-case areas, including biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and employment. For most Annex III systems the provider follows the internal-control procedure. For Annex III biometric systems, a notified body is needed where the provider has not fully applied harmonised standards or common specifications. Annex I lists the Union harmonisation legislation for products. Where the AI system is a safety component of an Annex I product, or is itself that product, and requires third-party conformity assessment, the provider follows that sectoral procedure, with one set of technical documentation and a single CE marking.

rows.question: What obligations apply to our general-purpose AI model?
rows.raw: Under Article 53(1), the provider of a general-purpose AI model must keep technical documentation of the model, including training, testing and evaluation results, at least as set out in Annex XI. It must also give providers who integrate the model the information and documentation set out in Annex XII, put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright, and publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the training content. Under Article 53(2), the two documentation duties do not apply to models released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters, but this exemption does not cover models with systemic risk. A model with systemic risk, presumed above 10^25 FLOPs of cumulative training compute, must also meet Article 55(1): model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, serious incident reporting to the AI Office, and adequate cybersecurity protection.

rows.question: What ongoing duties fall on a provider under Articles 72 and 73?
rows.raw: A provider of a high-risk AI system has two ongoing duties: post-market monitoring and serious incident reporting. Article 72(1) and (2) require a documented post-market monitoring system, proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks, that actively and systematically collects, documents and analyses relevant data from deployers or other sources to evaluate continuing compliance. Article 72(3) requires this system to rest on a post-market monitoring plan forming part of the technical documentation. Article 72(4) lets providers already covered by sectoral monitoring rules integrate these elements into existing plans, provided equivalent protection is achieved. Article 73 requires the provider to report any serious incident to the market surveillance authorities of the Member State where it occurred within 15 days of becoming aware of it, or within two days for a widespread infringement or critical-infrastructure disruption.

rows.question: What requirements are defined in Article 9 for high-risk systems?
rows.A: Article 9 requires a risk management system for high-risk AI systems that is established, implemented, documented and maintained (Article 9(1)). It must run as a continuous iterative process over the whole lifecycle, with regular systematic review (Article 9(2)). That process must cover four steps. identifying and analysing the known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights; estimating and evaluating risks under the intended purpose and under reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluating other risks found in post-market monitoring data; adopting targeted risk management measures. It covers only risks that can reasonably be mitigated or eliminated through development, design or technical information (Article 9(3)). Weighing and residual risk. The measures must take into account the combined effects of the requirements (Article 9(4)). They must also make residual risk acceptable through elimination by design, mitigation and control measures, and information and training for deployers (Article 9(5)). Testing. Testing must identify the right measures and confirm consistent performance (Article 9(6)). It may take place in real world conditions (Article 9(7)). It must happen before the system is placed on the market, against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds (Article 9(8)). Other duties. Providers must consider the impact on persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Article 9(9)). They may combine these procedures with risk management procedures required under other Union law (Article 9(10)).

rows.question: What risk categories exist under the EU AI Act?
rows.raw: The EU AI Act sets up four risk tiers. Prohibited practices under Article 5 are banned outright, and there are eight of them, including social scoring and untargeted facial-image scraping. High-risk systems are classified under Article 6, either as a safety component or product covered by Annex I legislation that requires third-party conformity assessment, or as an Annex III use case. Limited risk systems carry the transparency obligation of Article 50, which covers AI interaction disclosure and marking of synthetic content, and minimal risk systems have no mandatory obligations. Running in parallel, Chapter V regulates general-purpose AI models: baseline duties apply to all of them, and stricter duties apply to models with systemic risk, presumed above 10^25 FLOPs of training compute.

rows.question: What specific obligations apply to deployers of these systems?
rows.raw: Article 26 requires deployers of high-risk AI systems to use them in accordance with the instructions for use, assign human oversight to competent and trained natural persons, and monitor operation. Where a risk arises they must inform the provider and the market surveillance authority and suspend use, and they must report serious incidents to the provider first. Deployers must keep the logs under their control for at least six months, and employers must inform workers' representatives and affected workers before putting a system into service at the workplace. Under Article 27, deployers that are public bodies or private entities providing public services must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, but this does not apply to critical-infrastructure systems.

rows.question: What steps are required under Articles 43 and 49 before a high-risk AI system is placed on the market?
rows.raw: The provider must complete a conformity assessment under Article 43 and then register under Article 49 before placing the system on the market. Under Article 43(1), biometric high-risk systems use internal control where harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied in full, and otherwise need a notified body to assess the quality management system and the technical documentation. Under Article 43(2), the other listed use cases use internal control without a notified body, and Article 43(3) folds product-embedded systems into the conformity assessment required by their sectoral legislation. Article 43(4) requires a new conformity assessment after any substantial modification. Under Article 49(1), the provider or authorised representative must then register itself and the system in the EU database, while critical-infrastructure systems register at national level under Article 49(5).

rows.question: What transparency obligation applies to AI-generated synthetic medical images used to augment a training dataset?
rows.raw: **Article 50(2) is the transparency obligation that applies.** The provider of the AI system generating the synthetic medical images must mark them in a machine-readable format so they can be detected as artificially generated. Its technical solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible. The duty does not apply where the system only performs an assistive function for standard editing, does not substantially alter the input data or its meaning, or is authorised by law for criminal-offence purposes. The deployer's deep fake disclosure duty under Article 50(4) is generally not triggered, because images used only inside a training dataset are not shown to natural persons as authentic content.

rows.question: When do high-risk AI obligations apply?
rows.raw: High-risk AI obligations apply in two stages under Article 113. Under Article 113(2), the high-risk obligations for systems in the Annex III use-case areas apply from 2 August 2026. Those areas include biometrics, education, employment and migration, asylum and border control. Under Article 113(3)(c), the obligations for high-risk AI systems that are products, or safety components of products, covered by Union harmonisation legislation apply later, from 2 August 2027. Under Article 113(3)(b), the Chapter III Section 4 rules on notifying authorities and notified bodies have applied since 2 August 2025, so the conformity assessment infrastructure is in place before the high-risk obligations begin.

rows.question: Which Annex I legislation covers an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device?
rows.raw: An AI system that is a safety component of a medical device is covered by Annex I, Section A, point 11, which lists Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices. rows.question: Which EU AI Act article governs the reporting of serious incidents involving a high-risk AI system?
rows.raw:
Article 73 governs serious incident reporting. Under Article 73(1), providers of high-risk AI systems placed on the Union market must report any serious incident to the market surveillance authorities of the Member States where it occurred. Article 73(2) to (4) require the report immediately once a causal link, or a reasonable likelihood of one, is established, and no later than these limits after the provider or deployer becomes aware of the incident:

- **15 days** as the general limit.
- **Two days** for a widespread infringement or a serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure.
- **10 days** where a person has died.

Article 73(5) permits an incomplete initial report followed by a complete one. Article 73(6) then requires the provider to investigate without delay, including a risk assessment and corrective action, while cooperating with the competent authorities.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight of high-risk AI systems, and what does it require?
rows.raw: **Article 14** governs human oversight. It requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while they are in use, through measures matched to the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, either built in by the provider or identified by the provider for the deployer to implement. The people assigned to oversight must be able to understand the system's capacities and limitations and monitor its operation, stay aware of automation bias, correctly interpret the output, and decide not to use it or to disregard, override or reverse its output. They must also be able to intervene in its operation or halt it in a safe state using a 'stop' button. For remote biometric identification systems, Article 14(5) also requires at least two competent natural persons to separately verify an identification before the deployer acts on it, unless Union or national law considers this disproportionate for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum.

rows.question: Which high-risk areas does Annex III list, and how does Article 6(2) use them?
rows.raw: Annex III lists eight high-risk areas: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and workers' management, essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Article 6(2) makes an AI system high-risk where it falls within a use case listed under one of those areas, alongside the separate Article 6(1) product-safety route. Article 6(3) exempts an Annex III system that poses no significant risk of harm where it performs a narrow procedural task, improves a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or performs a preparatory task. A system that profiles natural persons always stays high-risk. Article 6(4) requires a provider relying on the exemption to document its assessment before placing the system on the market.

rows.question: Which information belongs in Annex VIII Section B?
rows.raw: Annex VIII Section B lists the information that a provider, or where applicable its authorised representative, must enter in the EU database under Article 49(2). This applies before placing on the market or putting into service an Annex III system that the provider has concluded is not high-risk under the derogation. Section B has nine items: the provider's name, address and contact details; the details of any person submitting on the provider's behalf; the authorised representative's details, where applicable; the AI system's trade name and any unambiguous reference allowing its identification and traceability; a description of its intended purpose; the derogation condition or conditions relied on; a short summary of the grounds for considering the system not high-risk; the system's status; and the Member States where it has been placed on the market, put into service or made available. The certificate, EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use items belong to Section A, not Section B.

rows.question: Which requirements apply to high-risk AI risk management and data governance?
rows.raw: Article 9 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to keep a documented risk management system, run as a continuous iterative process across the system's lifecycle, covering identification of known and reasonably foreseeable risks, estimation of risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluation of post-market monitoring data, and targeted risk management measures. Article 10 subjects training, validation and testing data sets to data governance practices covering design choices, data collection and origin, data preparation, assumptions, availability and suitability, bias examination and mitigation, and data gaps. It also requires those data sets to be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete, with special categories of personal data processed only where strictly necessary for bias detection and correction under appropriate safeguards.

rows.question: Which route applies if harmonised standards exist?
rows.raw: For a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III point 1 (biometrics), **Article 43(1)** lets the provider that has applied harmonised standards, or common specifications where applicable, choose the internal control procedure in **Annex VI** instead of the notified-body procedure. Under **Annex VI**, the provider itself checks that its quality management system complies with Article 17, examines the technical documentation, and verifies that design, development and post-market monitoring are consistent with it. No notified body is involved. Under Article 43(2), systems in Annex III points 2 to 8 always follow **Annex VI**, whether or not standards are applied. A notified body becomes mandatory for point 1 systems where standards are missing, applied only in part, or published with a restriction, or where common specifications exist but are not applied.

rows.question: obligations under Articles 13 and 50?
rows.raw: Article 13 requires high-risk AI systems to be transparent enough for deployers to interpret their output and use it appropriately, with instructions for use covering provider identity, intended purpose, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, foreseeable risks, human oversight measures, resources, expected lifetime, maintenance and log mechanisms. Under Article 50(1) and (2), providers must tell natural persons they are interacting with an AI system unless this is obvious, and mark synthetic content in a machine-readable form. Under Article 50(3) and (4), deployers must inform persons exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation and disclose deepfakes and AI-generated public-interest text, though the text duty does not apply to use authorised by law for criminal offences or to content under human editorial responsibility.

rows.question: what does art 13 require?
rows.raw: Article 13(1) requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed so that their operation is sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret the system's output and use it appropriately, with an appropriate type and degree of transparency. Article 13(2) requires the systems to come with instructions for use containing concise, complete, correct and clear information. Under Article 13(3), those instructions must cover the provider's identity and contact details, the intended purpose, the levels of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, the capabilities to explain output, performance on specific groups of persons, input data and data set specifications, pre-determined changes, human oversight measures, computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime and maintenance, and the mechanisms for collecting, storing and interpreting logs.
